description:
I'm Ibrahim Mursalin, a student from Mymensingh, Bangladesh, and the person behind Team Emberline. Right now the team is just me, and I'm looking for people to take TerraFlux further with me.

TerraFlux is a live web app that puts NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire detections on one grid, so the two sensors can be compared and the difference between them can be checked. It works today at https://terra-flux.vercel.app, and the code and method are public:
summary:
TerraFlux is a web app that puts NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire detections on one common grid so they can be compared. The two instruments count differently: for Bangladesh, VIIRS reports about 13 times more observations than MODIS (197,537 against 15,240 in the selected range), so raw counts cannot simply be added, and a change in a total can come from the satellite instead of the fire.

TerraFlux counts burning cell-days on a 0.15° grid (about 16.5 km), measures how the two sensors relate in the months when both fly, and scales MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent units. For Bangladesh the bridge has r² 0.808 over 69 validation months, with a typical error of about 53.0%. The app shows that error next to the numbers.

Users can explore detections on a 3D globe or a 2D map, read a monthly burning calendar, compare this month so far with earlier years, and open any day in NASA Worldview. The limits are on the page: detections are thermal anomalies, not confirmed fires, and clouds and revisit gaps hide some.

Built solo by Ibrahim Mursalin (Team Emberline, Mymensingh, Bangladesh) for the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots".
Live site: https://terra-flux.vercel.app
details:
What it does
MODIS (on the Terra and Aqua satellites, 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, 375 m pixels) both detect thermal anomalies from space, but they count them differently. For Bangladesh, VIIRS reports about 13 times more observations than MODIS (197,537 against 15,240 in the range I selected). TerraFlux puts both sensors in one view, so this difference can be read and checked instead of hidden.

How it works
I read the detections from NASA FIRMS and store them in a Supabase database. TerraFlux then counts burning cell-days: one 0.15° grid cell (about 16.5 km) with at least one detection on one UTC day. Each cell counts once per day, so pixel size no longer changes the count. In the months when both sensors are flying (at least 36 are required), I measure how they relate and scale MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent units. For Bangladesh on the Compare page, the scale k is 6.672, r² is 0.808 over 69 validation months, and the typical error is about 53.0% (leave-one-year-out). The app shows this error next to the numbers. Values from before the VIIRS overlap are estimates from this bridge. Raw counts are never added across sensors. Every number comes from stored query results, and METHODS.md in the repository explains each step.

What people can do
Explore shows detections on a 3D globe or a 2D map in five views: Native, Common grid, Harmonized, Anomaly and Agreement. It has playback through the days and a table of detections. The Calendar shows Bangladesh month by month from 2020 to 2026 and compares this month so far with earlier years, with the length of the baseline shown. Compare puts the two sensors side by side. Opening a day shows its detections and a link to NASA Worldview. The Methodology page says what TerraFlux can and cannot know.

Benefits and intended impact
I built it for people such as students, researchers and local analysts who want to ask whether this month is above normal, and to see how much of a difference may come from the sensor instead of the fire. It does not measure danger or predict fires.

What is creative
The bridge is made to be checked. A tooltip can always be compared with the displayed MODIS value and k, and the error sits beside the result.

Factors I considered
Detections are thermal anomalies, not confirmed fires. Clouds, smoke, gaps between satellite passes and near-real-time delay change what is seen. The MODIS confidence buckets are TerraFlux's own estimate, not an official NASA definition. TerraFlux does not use NASA logos and is not an official NASA product.

Tools and software
TypeScript, React 19, TanStack Start and Router, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui (built on Radix UI), Leaflet for the 2D map, three.js and react-globe.gl for the 3D globe, and Recharts for charts. Detections are stored in Supabase (Postgres, SQL and one Edge Function) and the app is hosted on Vercel. No special hardware was used; it runs in a web browser. Source code: https://github.com/mursalin999/TerraFlux

AI use
I used v0, and Claude to draft the interface and code and to write prompts. Claude also helped write this form and the demo slides. These tools did not create fire records or change NASA observations. I reviewed the interface, code, data handling and wording.

Next steps
Extend the record back to 2000, reduce the bridge error, and test TerraFlux with real users.
